ods00: Osmotic demyelination syndrome happens when chronic low sodium is corrected too fast.
ods01: Brain cells adapt to low sodium by shedding OZ-mo-lites. A rapid rise in sodium then pulls water out of them, and the myelin breaks down.
ods02: The central pons is hit hardest, where grey and white matter are tightly interwoven.
ods03: Symptoms are delayed, usually two to six days after the correction. Slurred speech, trouble swallowing, weakness in all four limbs, and in severe cases, locked-in syndrome.
ods04: On M-R-I, diffusion restriction comes first, within about a day. T-two and flair changes can lag by up to two weeks.
ods05: On axial T-two, look for a bright central pons shaped like a trident. The outer rim of the pons and the corticospinal tracts are spared.
ods06: It can also strike outside the pons. Look for symmetric signal in the basal ganglia and thalami.
ods07: Risk is highest with alcohol use disorder, malnutrition, liver disease, and low potassium.
ods08: Prevention is the treatment. In chronic hyponatremia, guidelines limit correction to about eight to ten millimoles per litre in any twenty-four hours.
ods09: Recently corrected sodium, and a trident in the pons? Think osmotic demyelination.
hod00: Hypertrophic olivary degeneration is a rare case where a damaged structure gets bigger, not smaller.
hod01: It starts with a circuit called the ghee-YAN moh-luh-RAY triangle. It links the red nucleus in the midbrain, the inferior olive in the medulla, and the dentate nucleus in the opposite cerebellum.
hod02: The dentate sends fibres up through the superior cerebellar peduncle, crossing to the red nucleus. The red nucleus connects down to the olive through the central tegmental tract.
hod03: A bleed, an infarct, or surgery that interrupts this pathway leaves the olive without its input.
hod04: Its neurons swell and vacuolate, so the olive enlarges.
hod05: On M-R-I, the olive in the front of the medulla turns bright on T-two about a month after the injury. It enlarges at around six months, and it does not enhance.
hod06: Years later the swelling settles and the olive shrinks, but the bright signal can persist.
hod07: Which side? A lesion in the central tegmental tract affects the olive on the same side. A cerebellar lesion affects the opposite olive.
hod08: The classic clinical sign is PAL-uh-tul tremor, a rhythmic movement of the soft palate.
hod09: A bright, enlarged olive, with an old lesion in the triangle? Don't call it a tumour.
bun00: Two parkinsonian syndromes, two classic M-R-I signs. The hot cross bun, and the hummingbird.
bun01: Multiple system atrophy combines parkinsonism, cerebellar ataxia, and autonomic failure, like fainting on standing and bladder problems.
bun02: In the cerebellar type, the transverse fibres of the pons and the midline RAY-fee degenerate, while the corticospinal tracts are spared.
bun03: On axial T-two, that leaves a bright cross in the pons. The hot cross bun sign. The pons and cerebellum also shrink.
bun04: It isn't specific. Some spinocerebellar ataxias show it too.
bun05: Progressive supranuclear palsy causes early falls, usually backwards, a stiff neck and trunk, and a vertical gaze palsy, especially looking down.
bun06: Here the midbrain shrinks, but the pons stays plump.
bun07: On the midline sagittal view, the thin midbrain forms the head and beak, and the pons forms the body. That's the hummingbird sign.
bun08: On axial images, the same midbrain atrophy gives the Mickey Mouse appearance.
bun09: A cross in the pons, think multiple system atrophy. A hummingbird midbrain, think progressive supranuclear palsy.
mbd00: mar-kee-uh-FAH-vuh been-YAH-mee disease is a rare disorder where the corpus cal-OH-sum breaks down.
mbd01: It's seen mainly in chronic alcohol use disorder and severe malnutrition, and is linked to B vitamin deficiency.
mbd02: Patients present with confusion, seizures, trouble walking, or coma. Chronic cases show dementia, and signs of disconnection between the two hemispheres.
mbd03: The damage targets the central layers of the corpus cal-OH-sum, and spares the thin layers above and below.
mbd04: On sagittal M-R-I, that gives the sandwich sign. A bright middle layer on T-two and flair, between preserved darker edges.
mbd05: The body is involved most often, then the JEN-yoo, then the SPLEE-nee-um.
mbd06: In the acute phase, the cal-OH-sum is swollen and can restrict diffusion.
mbd07: In the chronic phase, it thins out, and develops dark cystic cavities on T-one.
mbd08: Treatment is THIGH-uh-min and other B vitamins, plus nutrition and stopping alcohol. Early cases can partly reverse.
mbd09: Alcohol history, and a striped corpus cal-OH-sum? Think mar-kee-uh-FAH-vuh been-YAH-mee.
scd00: Subacute combined degeneration is spinal cord damage from vitamin B twelve deficiency.
scd01: Causes include pernicious anemia, stomach or bowel surgery, a strict vegan diet without supplements, and nitrous oxide use, which inactivates B twelve.
scd02: B twelve is needed to maintain myelin. Without it, the dorsal columns break down first, then the lateral corticospinal tracts. That's why it's called combined.
scd03: The dorsal columns carry vibration and joint position sense. So patients get tingling in the hands and feet, numbness, and an unsteady gait that's worse in the dark.
scd04: Corticospinal involvement adds weakness and stiffness.
scd05: On sagittal T-two, look for a long bright stripe along the back of the cord, usually in the cervical and upper thoracic segments.
scd06: On axial T-two, the two dorsal columns light up as an inverted V. It's also called the inverted rabbit ears sign.
scd07: Copper deficiency can look identical, so check copper too.
scd08: Treat early with B twelve replacement. Symptoms and signal changes can reverse if it's caught early.
scd09: Sensory ataxia, and an inverted V in the dorsal cord? Check the B twelve.
moya00: Moyamoya is a progressive narrowing of the arteries at the base of the brain. The name is Japanese for a puff of smoke.
moya01: The ends of both internal carotid arteries slowly narrow, along with the first parts of the anterior and middle cerebral arteries.
moya02: To compensate, tiny perforating arteries at the base of the brain enlarge into a tangle of collaterals.
moya03: On angiography, that tangle looks like a hazy puff of smoke.
moya04: On T-two M-R-I, look for small or absent flow voids at the carotid ends, and multiple tiny dark dots in the basal ganglia.
moya05: On flair and post contrast images, slow flow in PIE-ul collaterals outlines the sulci. That's the ivy sign.
moya06: Children usually present with ischemic strokes or transient attacks, often triggered by crying or hyperventilation. Adults can also bleed.
moya07: When there's no cause, it's moyamoya disease. The same pattern with a cause, like sickle cell disease, neurofibromatosis type one, Down syndrome, or cranial radiation, is moyamoya syndrome.
moya08: Treatment is surgical revascularisation, bypassing the narrowing using a scalp artery.
moya09: Narrowed carotid ends, with a puff of smoke? Think moyamoya.
tolosa00: toh-LOH-suh Hunt syndrome is a painful off-thal-mo-PLEE-juh, caused by idiopathic inflammation in the cavernous sinus.
tolosa01: The cavernous sinus sits beside the pituitary. It carries the internal carotid artery, plus cranial nerves three, four, six, and the first division of five.
tolosa02: Granulomatous inflammation there squeezes those nerves.
tolosa03: So patients get a severe, boring pain around one eye, then double vision, and sometimes a droopy lid or a numb forehead.
tolosa04: On M-R-I, look for soft tissue that widens one cavernous sinus, with a bulging lateral wall. It enhances with contrast, and can extend to the orbital apex.
tolosa05: It may also narrow the internal carotid artery as it passes through.
tolosa06: Symptoms improve dramatically with steroids. The pain often settles within seventy-two hours.
tolosa07: But it's a diagnosis of exclusion. Lymphoma, meningioma, sarcoidosis, metastases, fungal infection, and aneurysm can look similar, and some also respond to steroids.
tolosa08: So a follow-up M-R-I is needed to confirm that it resolves.
tolosa09: Painful off-thal-mo-PLEE-juh, and an enhancing cavernous sinus? Think toh-LOH-suh Hunt, after excluding the rest.
lisf00: The LIZ-frank injury is one of the most commonly missed injuries in the foot.
lisf01: The LIZ-frank joint is where the metatarsals meet the midfoot. The base of the second metatarsal is recessed between the kyoo-NEE-uh-forms, like the keystone of an arch.
lisf02: The LIZ-frank ligament runs from the medial kyoo-NEE-uh-form to the base of the second metatarsal. There's no ligament between the first and second metatarsal bases.
lisf03: The injury happens when a foot that's pointing down is loaded or twisted, like a fall, a car crash, or a football tackle.
lisf04: On the frontal view, the medial edge of the second metatarsal should line up with the medial edge of the middle kyoo-NEE-uh-form.
lisf05: On the oblique view, the medial edge of the fourth metatarsal should line up with the medial edge of the cuboid.
lisf06: Look for widening between the first and second metatarsal bases, and for a tiny bone chip in that gap. That's the fleck sign, an avulsion of the LIZ-frank ligament.
lisf07: Subtle injuries may only show on weight-bearing views. If suspicion stays high, get a C-T.
lisf08: Missed injuries lead to a collapsed arch and chronic pain, and many need surgical fixation.
lisf09: Midfoot pain, and a bruise on the sole? Check the second metatarsal alignment.
seg00: The seh-GOND fracture is a tiny chip of bone that signals a big knee injury.
seg01: It's an avulsion fracture from the lateral edge of the tibial plateau, just below the joint line.
seg02: It happens when the knee is forced into internal rotation and VAIR-us, usually during a pivoting sports injury.
seg03: The lateral capsule and the anterolateral ligament pull off a sliver of bone.
seg04: On a frontal knee x-ray, look for a thin, curved, vertical fragment beside the lateral tibial plateau. It's only a few millimetres wide.
seg05: Why does it matter? The same force tears the anterior cruciate ligament. An A-C-L tear is present in at least three quarters of cases.
seg07: So the next step is an M-R-I of the knee.
seg08: Don't confuse it with a reverse seh-GOND fracture. That one is on the medial side, and is linked to posterior cruciate ligament injury.
seg09: A tiny lateral tibial chip? Assume the A-C-L is torn until proven otherwise.
lun00: Perry-LOO-nate and LOO-nate dislocations are easy to miss, and both are emergencies.
lun01: They follow a high energy fall onto an outstretched hand, with the wrist bent back.
lun02: On a normal lateral view, three bones stack in a straight line. The radius, then the LOO-nate sitting on it like a cup, then the CAP-ih-tate sitting in the LOO-nate.
lun03: In a perry-LOO-nate dislocation, the LOO-nate stays in place on the radius. But the CAP-ih-tate, and the rest of the carpus, dislocate, usually dorsally.
lun04: In a LOO-nate dislocation, the LOO-nate itself is pushed out toward the palm, and tips forward. That's the spilled teacup sign. The CAP-ih-tate drops back in line with the radius.
lun05: On the frontal view, the smooth carpal arcs are broken, and the LOO-nate looks triangular, like a slice of pie.
lun06: Always look for an associated fracture. The SKAF-oyd waist is the most common.
lun07: The median nerve is at risk in the carpal tunnel, especially with a LOO-nate dislocation.
lun08: Both need urgent reduction, and usually surgical repair.
lun09: Check the lateral view. Radius, LOO-nate, CAP-ih-tate. If the line is broken, find which bone has moved.
